summary:
No measure, incident, arrest, ban or institution concerning trans visitors is recorded in Sinop itself in the audited sources. What a trans visitor to Sinop faces is the Turkish national framework, and no Sinop authority is documented adding enforcement or prohibitions of its own.

Sinop stands under the national framework of Turkey. Homosexuality was decriminalised in 1858 under the Ottoman penal code and legal gender change has been possible since 1988, but same-sex marriage is not recognised and LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military. Pride events have been repeatedly blocked by governors: the 2015–2018 Istanbul parades were banned by local authorities, and on 14 June 2019 the Istanbul, İzmir and Antalya prides were all banned by the cities' governors.

A proposal to criminalise publicly encouraging 'behavior contrary to biological sex' with a one-to-three-year prison sentence was ultimately not included in the 12th judicial package. Amnesty's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26) records three draft law packages made public in 2025 that would criminalise LGBTI identity expression and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible; none was submitted to parliament.

In June 2025 blanket bans were issued against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values'.
tangentialFactors:
The bans on pride marches were issued by the governors of Istanbul, İzmir and Antalya rather than by any Sinop authority, and the dissolution order came from an İzmir court. These are examples of how the national framework is applied by regional officials elsewhere in Turkey; a visitor to Sinop should read them as evidence of the enforcement climate rather than as measures in force in Sinop itself.

The draft law packages criminalising LGBTI identity expression and consensual same-sex relations, and the proposal on 'behavior contrary to biological sex' that was dropped from the 12th judicial package, indicate an active legislative direction. Whether any package has since been submitted to parliament is unresolved in the sources.
localsOnly:
Residents of Sinop live under the national framework: legal gender change has been available since 1988, same-sex marriage is not recognised, and LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military. No Sinop-specific restriction, protection measure or local ordinance concerning LGBTI residents is documented in the audited sources.

The repeated banning of pride marches by governors in other provinces signals the conditions under which a Sinop Pride event would likely be assessed, but no ban or permission decision concerning Sinop itself appears in the sources.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any of the three draft law packages made public in 2025 has since been submitted to parliament or enacted is unresolved in the sources.

The audited sources contain no incident, enforcement action, local ordinance or institutional practice recorded in Sinop itself; the assessment rests entirely on the national framework and on documented practice in other provinces.

The status of any LGBTI association, support organisation or medical provider operating within Sinop is not sourced.
